### Definition of "Determinism"

// Note: This subsection is generated by Claude. Need to check them by hand before finalizing!

Almost every agent framework calls something "deterministic". They rarely mean the same thing.

**System-level determinism (OMAR).** The system's behavior is a function of its inputs and its agents' outputs. Given the same agent writes, every run produces the same steps, at the same logical times, in the same order, with the same commits and the same routing. That includes concurrent work. The runtime guarantees it; it doesn't depend on the developer's discipline.

#### What the others mean

**Google ADK: routing determinism.** ADK describes its [workflow agents](https://adk.dev/agents/workflow-agents/) as producing "deterministic and predictable execution patterns", because code, not a model, picks the next sub-agent. That covers *which* agents run, not the order their results land in. ADK's own [parallel-agent docs](https://adk.dev/agents/workflow-agents/parallel-agents/) say the "event order is not deterministic", and parallel branches share session state.

**LangGraph: a replay requirement on your code.** LangGraph's [durable-execution docs](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/durable-execution) ask you to make your workflow "deterministic and idempotent" and to "wrap any side effects or non-deterministic operations inside tasks". On resume, it replays steps and reuses stored task results. Determinism here is a contract the developer keeps so that replay is consistent, not a property the runtime provides. And updates from parallel branches in one step ["may not be ordered consistently"](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-control-flow).

**Microsoft Agent Framework: a fixed graph, plus replayable orchestration.** In MAF, "deterministic workflows" means a fixed graph topology, as opposed to orchestrations where agents drive coordination. Its [Durable Task extension](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/durable-task/sdks/durable-agents-microsoft-agent-framework) checkpoints each agent call and recovers without re-running completed ones. That builds on Durable Task orchestrations, whose replay model requires orchestrator code to be deterministic, which is again a rule for the developer. Within a single step, the order of concurrent executors isn't fixed.

**Omnigent: deterministic policy enforcement.** Databricks' [Omnigent](https://www.databricks.com/blog/introducing-omnigent-meta-harness-combine-control-and-share-your-agents) enforces rules such as cost budgets and permissions "at the meta-harness layer, not via prompts", outside the model, so the model can't reason around them. That makes governance predictable, not coordination.

### The distinction, one line each

- **ADK:** *which step runs next* is decided by code.
- **LangGraph and MAF Durable:** *replay* reproduces a past run, provided your code is deterministic.
- **MAF workflows:** the *graph's shape* is fixed.
- **Omnigent:** *policy decisions* are made by code, not the model.
- **OMAR:** *the whole coordination* (routing, timing, concurrent ordering and commits) is reproducible and guaranteed by the runtime's semantics, so properties can be proved over every run.

The others each fix one layer and leave the rest, especially concurrent ordering, to chance or to the developer. System-level determinism closes all of those layers together.

The table below shows the requirements of achiving system-level determinism, with other frameworks in context.

| Requirement of system-level determinism | OMAR | LangGraph | Microsoft Agent Framework | Google ADK | Omnigent |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| The program, not a model, decides which step runs next | ✓ | ◐ | ✓ | ✓ | — |
| The graph can't change shape during a run | ✓ | ◐ | ✓ | ◐ | — |
| Concurrent results merge in a fixed order | ✓ | — | — | — | — |
| Shared state has no races | ✓ | ◐ | ◐ | — | — |
| Timing is logical, not wall-clock | ✓¹ | ◐ | ◐ | — | — |
| The runtime, not the prompt, limits what an agent may do | ✓ | — | ◐ | — | ✓² |
| Recovery resumes from a consistent point | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ◐ | ◐ |
| A past run can be replayed exactly | ◐³ | ✓⁴ | ✓ | ◐ | — |
| Guarantees are machine-checked for every run | ✓ | — | — | — | — |
| **Total** | **8 ✓ · 1 ◐** | 2 ✓ · 4 ◐ | 4 ✓ · 3 ◐ | 1 ✓ · 3 ◐ | 1 ✓ · 1 ◐ |

✓ the runtime guarantees it · ◐ partly, or only while the developer keeps a rule · — not provided

1. Except `within` deadlines, which use the wall clock.
2. Omnigent's policies cover cost, permissions and tool use, which OMAR's per-port write contracts don't.
3. OMAR has checkpoints and rollback. Replaying recorded writes is in its spec but not yet built.
4. Only if your code is deterministic and wraps side effects in tasks.

*Based on each project's public documentation as of November 2026.*
